claims.text: Increasing aluminum content in refractory high-entropy alloys promotes formation of a continuous protective Al2O3 scale at high temperature.
Formation of the Al2O3 scale substantially improves oxygen resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
The baseline refractory high-entropy alloy exhibits relatively high oxidation rates at extreme temperatures.
Increasing bulk aluminum content or applying an Al-rich surface treatment is the proposed intervention.
The proposed protective effect should operate during exposure at approximately 1200°C in air for 100 hours.
The intervention produces a continuous, dense, and adherent alumina scale on the alloy surface.
Added aluminum preferentially oxidizes at high temperature to form alumina.
The alumina scale acts as a barrier that limits further oxygen diffusion into the substrate.
Limiting oxygen diffusion reduces the overall oxidation rate.
The aluminum-modified alloy will have lower mass gain than the untreated alloy under the same exposure conditions.
The aluminum-modified alloy will exhibit improved oxide-scale integrity relative to the untreated alloy.
Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys form less protective and more porous oxide scales under the stated conditions.
Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys have higher oxidation rates than aluminum-modified alloys under the same conditions.
A sufficient aluminum supply is required to form a continuous alumina layer and obtain the protective effect.
The protective effect may not persist above approximately 1300°C.
Extremely oxygen-rich conditions may cause the alumina scale to spall or degrade.
